articles.title: NHL Power Rankings After the 1st Week of the 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: The Stanley Cup has never been won in October.
articles.body:
The Stanley Cup has never been won in October.

Nor has it ever been lost in autumn's first full month.

But with each of the NHL's 32 teams playing games, that is all the reason B/R's hockey staff needs to get together for the regular season's first installment of Power Rankings after the first week of the 2026-27 schedule.

Take a look at what we came up with and drop a thought in the app comments.

Statistics through games of Monday, Oct. 5.

ANA | BOS | BUF | CAR | CBJ | CGY | CHI | COL | DAL | DET | EDM | FLA | LAK | MIN | MTL | NJD | NSH | NYI | NYR | OTT | PHI | PIT | SEA | SJS | STL | TBL | TOR | UTA | VAN | VGK | WPG | WSH

Few expected them to be good, but did anyone really think it'd be this bad in Calgary, where the Flames are 0-3-0 after scoring three goals and allowing 16? "I feel like right now we're disconnected," coach Ryan Huska said . Also, former first-round pick Connor Zary (24th overall, 2020) was waived.

Connor Bedard got on the ice with his teammates for some drills and shots in practice, but he's still not cleared for contact after undergoing surgery on his left shoulder following an injury sustained in early July.

Did someone say overachievement? That's the revisionist vibe surrounding the Flyers, who were a 98-point playoff team in 2025-26 but started this year with four straight losses (while scoring just five goals) for the first time since 2014.

Players That Will Dominate the Rumor Mill

Two goals in two games (entering Tuesday) won't do it for the Red Wings, and it didn't help when they allowed three on the power play to Winnipeg. "Our guys are pi**ed when they are down," coach Todd McLellan said , "but they aren't digging graves, they are trying to dig themselves out of a hole."

A return for Dylan Larkin on Tuesday led to a win against Ottawa, but there's still plenty to sort through.

Starting goaltending was considered a mystery going in, and the numbers through two games showed why, as the Kings' tandem of Anton Forsberg and Darcy Kuemper allowed 13 goals on 54 shots (a .759 save percentage) in season-opening losses to Colorado (8-4) and San Jose (5-4).

It took 48 hours for the Devils to go from an OT win against Philadelphia to a 6-0 shellacking by the New York Islanders. "We were playing preseason hockey," coach Sheldon Keefe said , "against a team that was probably playing February-type hockey."

A home loss on Tuesday against Utah won't help matters for Keefe.

The Maple Leafs are getting exposure to close games early on, with each of the first three decided by a goal. The problem is, they lost twice. The good news? Newly acquired Kirill Marchenko scored his first with the team on Saturday and Gavin McKenna tallied his first NHL goal Tuesday in the OT win vs. Nashville.

That's more like it. The Stars were on the wrong end of 4-0 and 2-1 decisions to start the season, but they looked much more like themselves on Monday night, holding San Jose to just 13 shots in a 5-0 home victory.

They'd played just two games and scored only three goals entering Tuesday, but that didn't mean Predators forward Steven Stamkos couldn't continue to climb the league's all-time chart. The 36-year-old buried a power-play chance against Dallas for his 625th career goal, tying him for 17th on the NHL all-time list.

Returning home after a loss in Columbus was good for the Sabres, but it was even better when Jiri Kulich, who played just 12 games in 2025-26 thanks to a season-ending blood clot, scored a go-ahead goal in a win against Chicago. "It's hard to put into words how much he's been grinding," captain Rasmus Dahlin said .

Score four goals in a shutout win one night, allow six on 36 shots the next. Such is life for a team searching for its game, said Blues coach Jim Montgomery. "We're trying to become a consistent team in a lot of things that we want to be good at—aggression, taking away time and space," he said .

Things got off to a good start with a six-goal outburst in a win over Buffalo but quickly settled back to earth for the Blue Jackets in a 4-1 loss to visiting Utah, in which Columbus allowed three power-play goals. The team's penalty-kill percentage (76.0) ranked 28th in the league last season.

We'll always have the first couple of days of the season, right? That may be the mindset of Boston fans after the Bruins won their first two games but have since dropped consecutive 4-1 decisions at Minnesota and at home against Ottawa.

Go ahead and include Paul Cotter among the early season's biggest free-agent steals. The 26-year-old forward signed a one-year, $2.15 million deal on July 1 and scored four goals in his first four games with the Canucks.

The Islanders focused on details while killing five penalties in a defeat of visiting New Jersey, pleasing coach Pete DeBoer. "You want them to be rewarded for that commitment early," DeBoer said , "because it promotes a belief in what you're doing, and if you don't win games, then it's hard to build that."

It wasn't official, but it wasn't exactly a secret either. Regardless, Alex Ovechkin officially answered the "Is this his final season?" question on Monday when he told teammates he'll hang up his skates after 2026-27.

Being the defending Cup champs has a way of staving off the angst, but starting the season with consecutive home losses to Florida and Washington was certainly not what Carolina had in mind. A win came in game three, in OT, against Philadelphia, and the Canes followed it up on Tuesday with a victory in Montreal against the Habs in an Eastern Conference Final rematch.

The shudders emanating from South Florida on Monday may have been because the Panthers are in familiar territory with Aleksander Barkov on the shelf for 6-to-8 weeks.

The news got worse on Tuesday. There are now concerns about Brad Marchand after he suffered an apparent leg injury and was helped off the ice in the win over LA.

Seattle was 28th overall in per-game offense last season, but you'd never have known it from two early dates with Calgary, during which the Kraken hammered the Flames with 12 goals on 59 shots, including six on 27 shots in Sunday's home opener. "The energy was absolutely nuts in the arena," goalie Joey Daccord said .

Be gentle with your Sharks fan friends for the next little while. San Jose's hockey resurgence took a hit when Macklin Celebrini missed Monday night's game against Dallas because of a lower-body injury. Yikes.

Marc Gatcomb wasn't a headline signing last summer, but he scored his first goal in a Vegas sweater in timely fashion, providing a win over Vancouver. A veteran of 88 NHL games prior to this season, the 27-year-old signed a two-year deal worth $875,000 per year.

A four-goal loss in Midtown Manhattan wasn't an ideal start to 2026-27, but the Lightning bounced back with home wins over Washington and Philadelphia, outscoring both teams 7-2.

The Penguins won their first two games of 2026-27 and were two-thirds of the way through to win No. 3 against visiting Winnipeg on Monday before surrendering three third-period goals inside of five minutes in a 3-2 loss.

Opening on the road wasn't the worst thing for the returning Eastern finalists, who won in Toronto and got an OT point in a loss in Pittsburgh. The Canadiens dropped one to the Canes on Tuesday and will stay for four before visiting Washington on Oct. 14.

Going from Long Island to Utah is an adjustment, but it's all part of the job for Mammoth forward Anders Lee, who moved west as a free agent after 13 seasons with the New York Islanders and scored in his first game.

The Mammoth picked up a win Tuesday night in New Jersey and head up to Boston on Thursday.

Another year, another bid to be among the goal-scoring elites for Kyle Connor, who scored three goals in the Jets' first two games after registering 31 or more goals in each of the last five seasons, topping out at 47.

Call it the Evan Bouchard Revenge Tour. He was the league's top-scoring blue-liner last season but was not a Norris Trophy finalist. This season, he's already produced eight points in his first three games.

He's been one of the league's best goalies for a while, and now he's an offensive weapon, too. Igor Shesterkin became the first goalie in the Rangers' long history to score a goal when he netted one against Tampa Bay.

The certainties of life: Death, taxes, and the Ducks winning their annual home opener. Anaheim made it 11 in a row in dramatic fashion when it shook off a late tying goal by Florida's Brad Marchand and won it 3-2 on Mikael Granlund's power-play tally in the first minute of overtime.

Defenseman Jake Sanderson was placed on the early-season injury list and missed games Monday and Tuesday after leaving Ottawa's Saturday game against Toronto. Sanderson had 4:29 of ice time in six shifts against the Maple Leafs.

The Wild followed a winning recipe in their first two games, getting offense from Kirill Kaprizov (three goals) and Quinn Hughes (three points) and 45 saves on 47 shots from goalie Jesper Wallstedt. Wallstedt started 33 games last season and had a .916 save percentage while sharing time with Filip Gustavsson.

It seems like old times for the defending Presidents' Trophy winners, who opened with eight goals in a blowout of Los Angeles and followed with six more in a one-sided defeat of St. Louis. "It's definitely not going to be like this every single night," defenseman Cale Makar said , "but it's good to start the season like it."

articles.title: Making the Case For Every Wrestler in WWE Money in the Bank 2026 Ladder Matches
articles.summary: WWE Money in the Bank is one of the most unpredictable nights on the wrestling calendar, with a championship opportunity hanging above the ring and 12 Superstars willing to do whatever it takes to win.
articles.body:
WWE Money in the Bank is one of the most unpredictable nights on the wrestling calendar, with a championship opportunity hanging above the ring and 12 Superstars willing to do whatever it takes to win.

Both the men's and women's ladder matches feature a mix of established stars, rising talents, and potential breakout performers, making it hard to count anyone out and even harder to figure out who walks away with the briefcase.

Here is the case for every Superstar competing to win Money in the Bank 2026.

Why Your Favorite Star Will Lose MITB Ladder Matches 😔

Breakker has an imposing combination of youth, speed and explosive power, and this stipulation gives him plenty of opportunities to turn those attributes into chaos.

WWE has already established Breakker as someone who deserves to be booked at the top of the card, so winning the briefcase would be another step toward making him one of the company's centerpiece stars instead of an experiment.

With his aerial expertise, Evans should be the most entertaining wrestler in the building. He has the kind of athleticism that makes a Money in the Bank match perfect for him, and his willingness to take risks could make him the Superstar everyone remembers when the match is over.

Evans also has something to prove, and a win would instantly establish that he is more than an exciting young prospect and is ready to become a major player.

Williams already carries himself like a future main eventer, which makes the briefcase a natural fit. He has the charisma, physical presence and confidence to make a championship chase feel important.

As the reigning United States champion, he already has momentum, and winning Money in the Bank would give WWE another way to elevate him without immediately forcing him into a world title reign.

The question now is whether WWE has the confidence to accelerate his rise this quickly.

Penta might have the strongest argument of anyone in the men's match. He has already been involved in the World Heavyweight Championship picture, has the experience to survive a chaotic ladder match, and has the personality to make a potential cash-in feel like a major event.

His recent championship opportunity against Roman Reigns also gives him the credibility several of his opponents don't have.

Penta does not need the briefcase to become a star, but the briefcase could turn him into a world champion.

Never underestimate the value of putting a briefcase in the hands of someone who understands exactly how much leverage it provides.

Punk won Money in the Bank in 2008 and 2009 and successfully cashed in both contracts, giving him firsthand knowledge of how to turn the briefcase into a world championship.

He has been around long enough to know how to manipulate a title opportunity, and his experience gives him a major advantage in a match where patience can matter as much as athleticism.

In addition, The Best in the World brings instant credibility to the contract, as his cash-in wouldn't feel like a surprise simply because he won Money in the Bank; it would feel like WWE deliberately put a dangerous weapon in his hands.

Owens is the ultimate wild card. He can fight, brawl, improvise and absorb punishment better than almost anyone in the field, and those qualities make him particularly dangerous in a ladder match.

More importantly, KO has a history of making championship programs feel personal.

If WWE wants a Money in the Bank winner who can turn the briefcase into an unpredictable storyline rather than simply a guaranteed title shot, Owens is a viable threat.

Ruca could be the breakout star of this year's women's match. She has the athletic ability to create spectacular moments on ladders and represents exactly the type of younger Superstar WWE can elevate with a Money in the Bank victory.

A win would give Ruca immediate storyline direction and give WWE a fresh face in the championship picture.

If the goal is to create a star rather than reward an established one, Ruca is the choice.

Vice's biggest argument is that she has almost nothing to lose. She is still establishing herself on the main roster, so a Money in the Bank victory could completely change her career trajectory.

Her striking-heavy style also gives her a different feel from several other competitors, as she doesn't need to outwrestle everyone to win; she needs to survive long enough to find an opening in a match built around opportunism.

Jayne already has championship gold around her waist, which could make her an unconventional choice, but that is also part of the appeal.

Winning Money in the Bank while holding the Women's United States Championship would immediately create questions about her ambitions and whether she intends to pursue an even bigger prize.

Jayne has shown she can thrive without being the most physically dominant person in the ring, which sets up the ladder match perfectly.

Perez should be the favorite in the women's match. She has already established herself as one of WWE's most dependable young performers and has previous Money in the Bank experience.

What matters in this contest is that knowing when to climb can be just as important as knowing how to fight, and Perez has the wrestling ability to survive the opening chaos, the intelligence to pick her spots, and enough credibility that a championship cash-in would immediately feel important.

Legend has the size and athleticism to change the match dynamic completely. She is not just another big competitor who can throw people around; she is an explosive athlete capable of doing things that should not be possible for someone her size. That makes her particularly dangerous once the ladders come into play.

WWE also has a chance to turn Legend's Money in the Bank victory into a genuine arrival moment, and a memorable performance could make her impossible to ignore.

Stratton has the best combination of experience, star power and storyline potential in the entire women's field. She has already won Money in the Bank once and successfully used that opportunity to become WWE women's champion, so she knows what the briefcase can do for a career.

She has the athleticism to excel in the match and enough personality to make another championship chase compelling.

If WWE wants to establish that Stratton is entering another major phase of her career, another Money in the Bank victory would accomplish that.

articles.title: Ranking the 10 Best Browns Players of All Time
articles.summary: Ranking the greatest Cleveland Browns players of all time is an exercise in celebrating the rich history of a franchise that goes all the way back to 1946.
articles.body:
Ranking the greatest Cleveland Browns players of all time is an exercise in celebrating the rich history of a franchise that goes all the way back to 1946.

The Browns might not have had the most premium talent over the last 25 years, but ranking the top 10 means sifting through 18 players in the Hall of Fame and the team's Ring of Honor.

Cleveland has yet to win a Super Bowl, but the franchise won eight championships between 1946 and 1964. Many of the players on this list were pivotal to those title runs, while others etched their names in franchise history without winning a championship.

Factoring in accolades, awards, production and impact on the franchise's history, here are the 10 best Browns players of all time.

The Snapshot: A defining defensive star for one of the most successful eras in Browns history. Matthews was a consistent leader of the defense for 16 seasons.

Claim to Fame: His stretch of four Pro Bowl seasons in five years coincided with a five-year stretch where the franchise reached three AFC Championship games. He's still No. 3 on the franchise's all-time sacks list with 75.

The Body of Work: Franchise's all-time leader in Approximate Value (125). 1,430 career tackles. Four-time Pro Bowler and one-time second-team All-Pro selection. Led the NFL in tackles four times.

The Catch: Matthews and Myles Garrett are the only players on this list who haven't been inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Matthews' inclusion is more about his longevity and role in the most modern run of postseason success for the Browns.

The Snapshot: Bulldozing pulling guard who was a constant in one of the league's best rushing attacks.

Claim to Fame: Paved the way for three different Hall of Fame running backs, including Jim Brown. Elite contributor to the 1964 championship season. The Browns never had a losing season during his career.

The Body of Work: Played 202 games in a 15-year career. Was named a first-team All-Pro in the middle of a six-year run of Pro Bowl nominations. Pro Football Hall of Famer, Browns' Ring of Honor inductee and All-Decade Team selection.

The Catch: It's hard to judge an interior lineman from his era with no statistical evidence of what he did. The highlights are excellent and the overall run game statistics help, but it's hard to separate his individual contribution.

The Snapshot: A dominant dual-threat tight end who balanced blocking and receiving duties in an era where few tight ends were doing both.

Claim to Fame: Retired as the career leader among tight ends in receptions (662) and receiving yards (7,980), with 47 touchdown catches. Led the team in receiving for five consecutive seasons from 1981 to 1985.

The Body of Work: Still leads the franchise in receiving yards despite playing well before the modern passing revolution. Two-time first-team All-Pro and three-time Pro Bowler. Pro Football Hall of Famer and member of the 1980s All-Decade Team.

The Catch: Newsome was a part of the Browns' successful run in the late 1980s, but he was past his prime at that point. The bulk of his productive years weren't spent on winning teams.

The Snapshot: The other Hall of Fame tailback from the 1960s. It's not easy to be the guy who follows the guy , but Kelly was a great successor to Jim Brown with a 10-season career in Cleveland.

Claim to Fame: Kelly served as Brown's backup for the first two years of his career and proceeded to rip off six consecutive Pro Bowl seasons. He was also the MVP runner-up in 1968.

The Body of Work: Kelly put up 9,555 yards from scrimmage with 87 rushing and receiving touchdowns. He was a three-time first-team All-Pro who led the NFL in rushing twice and rushing touchdowns three years in a row.

The Catch: Kelly acknowledged his goal was to be one of the best backs in the league, not a "superman" like Jim Brown. He carried the torch, but his rushing production declined after his first three seasons as a starter, and the Browns never reached the same heights they had with Brown.

The Snapshot: The man who came before Jim Brown. Motley was the original star running back for the franchise and a centerpiece for an offense that won four AAFC Championships and an NFL title in 1950.

Claim to Fame: A pioneer for the organization, Motley and teammate Bill Willis broke the AAFC's color barrier in 1946, the same year Kenny Washington and Woody Strode reintegrated the NFL. Motley led the AAFC in rushing in 1948 and the NFL in 1950.

The Body of Work: Pro Football Hall of Fame inductee, member of the 1940s All-Decade team and two-time first-team All-Pro selection. Motley averaged 6.4 yards per touch. The overall production, 4,712 rushing yards and 31 touchdowns, isn't up there with Brown or Kelly, but his significance on championship teams gives him a boost.

The Catch: Part of Motley's resume includes his willingness and ability as a blocker. Legendary coach Paul Brown described him as "completely unselfish." It's hard to quantify his work as a blocker, pioneer and leader.

The Snapshot: Game-wrecking edge-rusher who is well on his way to donning a Gold Jacket in Canton. There aren't many modern Browns who have reached that level.

Claim to Fame: Set the single-season sack record (23) in 2025, earning his second Defensive Player of the Year Award. In short, he's been one of the few reasons for fans to tune in to Browns games over the last nine years.

The Body of Work: His total of 125.5 sacks in a Browns uniform is tied with Dwight Freeney for 20th all time. Five-time first-team All-Pro selection in his nine seasons with Cleveland. Garrett is one of the most prolific sack artists of his era.

The Catch: Many on this list were key players for some of the best Browns teams. That's not the case for Garrett. For all of his individual accolades, Cleveland had just two winning seasons with him on the roster.

The Snapshot: The embodiment of what an NFL offensive lineman is supposed to be for over a decade. Thomas was the standard for left tackle play throughout his 11-year career.

Claim to Fame: Hall of Famer who logged 10,363 consecutive snaps while maintaining elite play year in and year out. Thomas was fiercely loyal to the organization despite a lack of team success he had little control over.

The Body of Work: Six-time first-team All-Pro selection. Was named the second-team left tackle on the All-PFF team over the last 20 years. Voted to the Pro Bowl in all but his final season. Maintained an elite level of play despite blocking for 20 different starting quarterbacks .

The Catch: Thomas was the best left tackle in the league for an extended stretch. However, even his elite pass protection wasn't enough to help the Browns achieve sustained team success during his career.

The Snapshot: Imagine combining Joe Thomas and Phil Dawson into one player, then add eight championships to his resume. Groza was a Hall of Fame offensive tackle and kicker for some of the best Browns teams ever.

Claim to Fame: Groza remains the Browns' all-time scoring leader with 1,608 points. He's the only player to be on the roster for all eight of the franchise's championships between the AAFC and NFL.

The Body of Work: Groza was a nine-time Pro Bowler and the starting tackle in six of those. Six All-Pro selections as a tackle. Made the field goal in the final seconds to deliver the 1950 NFL championship over the Los Angeles Rams.

The Catch: Groza was considered to be a top-tier tackle in his prime, but he was a kicker only from 1961 to 1967. His ranking here is more about the longevity of a 21-year career than absolute domination at his peak.

The Snapshot: Paul Brown's handpicked quarterback to lead the early Browns dynasty. Graham was an elite quarterback in the team's AAFC and early NFL days.

Claim to Fame: Quarterback for the franchise's first 10 seasons, leading Cleveland to the championship game every year. Graham executed Paul Brown's offense at an elite level and threw for 23,584 yards and 174 touchdowns with 44 more touchdowns on the ground.

The Body of Work: Earned all-league honors in nine of his 10 professional seasons. He averaged 9.0 yards per passing attempt across his AAFC and NFL career. He was the starting quarterback for seven of the Browns' eight championships across the two leagues.

The Catch: Very little. Graham was exactly what constituted a star quarterback in his era and is one of the two most accomplished players in franchise history.

The Snapshot: The team isn't actually named for him, but it might as well be. Brown is a mythical figure in Browns history and one of the all-time greats regardless of franchise.

Claim to Fame: Brown led the league in rushing in eight of his nine seasons. He was a three-time NFL MVP and the engine that led the Browns to their last championship in 1964.

The Body of Work: Still ranks 12th all-time in rushing yards with 12,312 despite only playing nine seasons. Eight-time first-team All-Pro selection and nine-time Pro Bowler. Holds the NFL record for rushing yards per game with 104.3.

The Catch: There is no catch with Brown. There is only greatness.

articles.title: 10 Athletes We'd Want to See Play Other Pro Sports
articles.summary: Given the talent and drive required to become a professional athlete, it's no surprise that many standouts also starred in another sport.
articles.body:
Given the talent and drive required to become a professional athlete, it's no surprise that many standouts also starred in another sport.

In some cases, we merely imagine a hypothetical. For example, Harry Kane is a world-class striker who's scored hundreds of goals for England and some of the biggest clubs. He recently floated the possibility of eventually kicking in the NFL.

For plenty of star athletes, we already have evidence of second-sport excellence, but we're left wondering what might have been.

We've highlighted 10 of the best examples here.

Without a doubt, Tom Glavine made the correct choice. He was a star pitcher for the Atlanta Braves, winning two Cy Young Awards and an MLB title—as the World Series MVP—en route to being a first-ballot Hall of Famer.

Glavine also could have chased a career on the ice.

As a senior in high school, he racked up 47 goals and 47 assists for a state-high 94 points, per David Pevear of the Lowell Sun . Glavine, who totaled 229 points in his Massachusetts high school career, then heard his name called as a fourth-round selection of the Los Angeles Kings in the 1984 NHL draft.

Glavine chose to sign with Atlanta, which helped develop the southpaw into the legendary 300-game winner whom we remember on the mound.

Tony Gonzalez's basketball career solidified his NFL future.

Back in 1997, Kansas City Chiefs coach Marty Schottenheimer and general manager Carl Peterson went to scout Gonzalez at the University of California. The star tight end doubled as a forward who averaged 6.4 points and 4.3 rebounds over three seasons.

"Any time he went up for a rebound in traffic, he would come down with the ball," Peterson later said of Gonzalez. "We thought that ability would be useful playing for the Chiefs, and it was."

Gonzalez pulled in 1,325 receptions for 15,127 yards and 111 touchdowns, all of which were NFL records for a tight end at the time of his retirement. Each one also remains a top-10 mark in NFL history regardless of position.

Julius Peppers is a member of both the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame. He starred for North Carolina, then entered the NFL as the No. 2 pick of the 2002 draft and dazzled with the Carolina Panthers, Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers.

Before he committed to flying off the edge, though, Peppers was a valuable piece of the iconic UNC basketball program.

As a freshman, he was a regular contributor on a Final Four team. Peppers averaged 7.1 points and 4.0 rebounds in his sophomore year—the last season he played prior to focusing on football.

"I'll tell you this, I do believe if Pep would've just focused on basketball, he could've played in the NBA," said Matt Doherty, who coached Peppers at UNC and later worked for the Indiana Pacers.

Peppers settled for registering the fifth-most sacks (159.5) in NFL history.

Ranking 10 Best Bills Players of All Time

NBA Players with the All-Time Most Career Earnings💰

Joe Mauer was just awesome at everything, huh?

While in high school, he earned a 5-star recruiting billing and committed to Florida State for football, twice earned Minnesota all-state recognition in basketball and shattered records on the diamond.

Mauer averaged 20-plus points for the basketball team, but he straight-up dominated as a quarterback. He threw for 3,022 yards with 41 touchdowns in his senior year, landing the USA Today National Player of the Year honors.

Oh, and the Minnesota Twins used the No. 1 pick of the 2001 MLB draft on Mauer.

Highlighted by the 2009 AL MVP, he further stuffed that impressive trophy case with three Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers. Mauer is only the third catcher in MLB history to become a first-ballot Hall of Fame selection.

When you're in the conversation for the greatest player of all time in your sport, any regrets about not playing a different sport are entirely unnecessary.

That's a common question for LeBron James, who collected 103 catches for 2,065 yards and 23 touchdowns in two years of high school football. He was an Ohio all-state selection in both seasons.

LeBron hung up his cleats as a senior to focus on basketball. Still, he shared that during the 2011 NBA lockout, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones and Seattle Seahawks coach Pete Carroll both contacted him about playing football.

If nothing else, it's fun to envision 6'8" LeBron constantly soaring over defenders in the end zone.

The comparison is not like-for-like, but NFL icon Antonio Gates provides an ideal transition from NBA legend LeBron.

During the same draft year (2003), Gates made the switch to football. He'd exclusively played basketball in college and was a key scorer for Kent State during its surprise run to the 2002 Elite Eight. Gates wrapped up his basketball career with 20.6 points, 7.7 rebounds and 4.1 assists per game as a senior.

The decision to focus on football worked out for him beautifully.

Gates joined the San Diego Chargers and quickly rose to stardom, securing first-team AP All-Pro honors in his second, third and fourth NFL seasons.

Gates stayed with the Chargers for 16 years, amassing 955 catches for 11,841 yards and 116 touchdowns—the last of which is still a top-10 all-time total.

The fork in the profession road led Jeff Samardzija to baseball.

Ultimately, he put together a 13-year MLB career that included an All-Star nod in 2014. Samardzija posted an 80-106 record with a 4.15 ERA and notched 1,449 strikeouts. Even though he didn't meet the expectations of a $90 million contract later in his career, Samardzija was a quality pitcher.

After retiring, he made it abundantly clear that baseball was the correct choice for him. Nevertheless, we can daydream about the former Notre Dame receiver taking the NFL route instead.

Samardzija made 77 receptions for 1,249 yards and 15 scores and was a second-team AP All-American (alongside a guy named Calvin Johnson) in 2005. He followed with 78 catches for 1,017 yards and 13 total touchdowns in 2006, leaving Notre Dame as the program's career leader in all three categories.

The most notable piece of Russell Wilson's story is how flirting with baseball directly altered his football career.

After the Colorado Rockies chose him in the fourth round of the 2010 MLB draft, Wilson totaled 3,998 offensive yards and 37 touchdowns as North Carolina State's quarterback that season. He wanted to play minor league ball the next summer—and did—which led to NC State moving on and Wisconsin swooping in.

Wilson parlayed a strong year at Wisconsin into a third-round selection by the Seattle Seahawks in the 2012 NFL draft. Nearly 47,000 passing yards and a Super Bowl ring later, Wilson had a terrific career at QB.

As with the others, there's no guarantee he would have flourished in the secondary sport. Wilson hit .228 in that summer with low-A Asheville.

But if Wilson had elected to focus solely on baseball, who knows?

The highest-profile case in recent memory, Kyler Murray holds the distinction of being a first-round selection in the MLB and NFL drafts.

In the summer of 2018, the Oakland Athletics picked him No. 9 overall. Months later, Murray threw for 4,000 yards and rushed for 1,000 more—making him only the second college QB to achieve that in a season—while leading Oklahoma to a Big 12 title and trip to the College Football Playoff.

Murray had said he planned to chase the NFL, and that fantastic year cemented his path to football. He went to the Arizona Cardinals at No. 1 overall, won Offensive Rookie of the Year and has surpassed $200 million in career earnings.

Still, in his final baseball season at OU, Murray hit .296 with 10 homers, 47 RBI, 16 more extra-base hits and 10 steals. He had serious upside on the diamond.

Russell Wilson appeared in the minors. Kyler Murray kept playing in college. A.J. Brown, on the other hand, essentially saw his baseball career end in high school.

Because he signed with the San Diego Padres as their 19th-round selection in 2016, Brown—an Under Armour All-American in two sports, as Murray was—could not suit up for Ole Miss baseball. He made a couple of brief stops at San Diego's extended spring training, but that was it.

However, those who watched him at the ballpark left impressed.

"The ball-hawking skill, the way he can go up and make a catch—he was like that in center field," Padres scout Stephen Moritz said . "His first steps might not have always been perfect. But he had this innate ability to track a ball down."

Brown has showcased that talent for eight seasons in the NFL, recording six 1,000-yard campaigns and counting. He also won a Super Bowl ring with the Philadelphia Eagles in 2024.

articles.title: Why Your Favorite Star Will Lose WWE Money in the Bank Ladder Matches
articles.summary: WWE presents its annual Money in the Bank premium live event from New Orleans on Saturday night, with competitors in the men's and women's ladder matches vying for contracts that guarantee each winner a world title opportunity at a time of their choosing within the next year.
articles.body:
WWE presents its annual Money in the Bank premium live event from New Orleans on Saturday night, with competitors in the men's and women's ladder matches vying for contracts that guarantee each winner a world title opportunity at a time of their choosing within the next year.

Anticipation builds as fans wait to see which Superstars will outlast their opponents, retrieve their respective briefcases, and set themselves up for a career-defining moment.

That is why I am here to put my hater hat on and tell you exactly why each competitor will not win their match, including two who will absolutely, positively, most definitely not capture the briefcase this weekend in the Big Easy.

The Prodigy has momentum on her side after WWE Creative finally realized she has been part of the main roster for over a year now, with two ongoing rivalries across Raw and AAA.

Despite that, though, the only way Perez wins this one is if Liv Morgan regains the Women's World Championship and the long-term plan is for her to cash in on her Judgment Day teammate.

Considering how long it took the powers that be to do anything of substance with her in the first place, I wouldn't hold my breath that she leaves New Orleans with the briefcase.

The NXT export is still finding her footing on the main roster, and the creative team is selective about which stars it worries about shoving down the audience's throats ( right, Bron Breakker ?). For the former MMA competitor, a guaranteed title opportunity would be premature.

A more realistic triumph is over Raquel Rodriguez for the Women's Intercontinental Championship.

Legend has been booked tremendously in her big-match appearances, looking like a world beater each time.

The follow-up has been lackluster, though, and the former pro basketball player has shown no real progress since her Royal Rumble and Elimination Chamber performances.

Unless Triple H and Co. are planning a massive surprise for the next season of WWE Unreal, expect Legend to look great, smash some fools, and then lose … like always.

The Fatal Influence leader is probably the most likely to win the match, which is why she will not.

The women's United States champion has been fast-tracked for main roster success since she, Fallon Henley and Lainey Reid arrived on SmackDown, and justifiably so.

Expect her teammates to make their presence felt, but expect Jayne to take a big bump onto a table that probably won't break—or through a ladder that inexplicably will—and lose the match dramatically.

The only woman in the match to previously win the briefcase, Stratton makes sense as she has become close to Chelsea Green, and there is plenty of storytelling to be had as a result.

And therein lies why Stratton will not win.

The current creative regime has never met a swerve it did not love or an opportunity to outthink the fans it did not take. If it decides Stratton is the most logical winner, it will book her to lose here and find another way to put her and Green on a collision course.

Expect a spectacular aerial spot but another "L" for Tiffy in New Orleans.

Which brings us to the competitor least likely to win the women's match Saturday night…

Definitely Not Winning The Most: Sol Ruca

Did you see how quickly they took the Women's Intercontinental Championship off Ruca and gave it to Raquel Rodriguez, only to do little with Rodriguez as champion?

Ruca has a bright future and has been much better in recent weeks, but her booking since the star-making rivalry with Lynch gives me little reason to expect WWE to position her for a world title shot against Stephanie Vaquer, Becky Lynch or Liv Morgan.

If her previous ladder matches in NXT are any indication, Ruca could well steal the show on Saturday night. She is a wildly talented athlete, but she definitely will not be lugging the briefcase around airports for the foreseeable future.

Owens carrying the briefcase and taunting former best friend Sami Zayn with it for a few weeks or months would be tremendous fun, but that does not feel like the direction WWE Creative is headed with him.

There is unfinished business with another participant in this year's Money in the Bank match, which should factor into his fate in Saturday's contest.

Do expect to cringe or shout at least once, though, as Owens has a rich history of teeth-grinding bumps in these kinds of matches.

It is too early for Williams to win the briefcase.

Sure, WWE Creative has dropped hints in backstage confrontations that Williams is coming for the top prize in the company, but he just got the United States title back, and forcing any further of a push at this point would feel counterproductive considering how popular he already is.

Trick will be world champion one day, but not now.

Evans has evolved his game so quickly in recent months that if I had the book, I would at least consider giving him the briefcase, building his star power over the coming months, and booking a surprise cash-in sometime next summer.

I am not Triple H, though, so expect The Young OG to steal the show, wow the fans, take a monster bump, and lose.

However, Evans has been all over TV, so the prospect of him eventually hitting the main event scene is not out of the question.

In a perfect world, Penta would score the win in his second major ladder match this year, capture the briefcase and cash in on Roman Reigns in the near future to capitalize on his unprecedented popularity and momentum.

While the luchador has to be considered a favorite to win the men's briefcase, he has already cooled down somewhat from his September 14 close call against The OTC.

The crowd will be behind him, but expect another near miss for the veteran competitor.

On paper, this is Breakker's match to win. He was reheated over the summer by way of his rivalry with Oba Femi, and if there was ever a time to give him the briefcase, it's now.

As noted, Triple H and the creative team are clearly terrified of shoving Breakker down the audience's collective throat. They have, after all, shown such remarkable restraint in pushing the second-generation competitor into the stratosphere.

Breakker may well leave New Orleans with the briefcase, but until it happens, I refuse to believe it.

Speaking of not believing it, there is one more Superstar who definitely will not be leaving Money in the Bank with the briefcase for the third time in his Hall of Fame career...

Definitely Not Winning the Most: CM Punk

This is no knock on Punk by any means. He is a guy who can walk right into the main event picture tomorrow, challenge for a title and win it.

He is as believable and legitimate a top Superstar as there is in WWE, and his days of having to win briefcases to justify title shots are way behind him.

One of the best wrestlers in WWE history, he is fresh off his latest run with the gold, and winning the briefcase Saturday night does nothing to boost him in any way.

It does not even serve as a means of propelling a storyline forward. It would be a win for a win's sake and little more.

Look for his rivalry with Kevin Owens to rear its head and take both men out, or perhaps a cameo by a desperate Sami Zayn to prevent Punk from earning another shot.

Either way, The Best in the World will not be carrying the briefcase out of New Orleans on Saturday.

articles.title: F1 Driver Valtteri Bottas Posts Video, Photos of 217-Mile Bike Ride to Singapore Grand Prix
articles.summary: Formula 1 driver Valtteri Bottas took the scenic route while traveling to race for Cadillac in the Singapore Grand Prix.
articles.body:
Formula 1 driver Valtteri Bottas took the scenic route while traveling to race for Cadillac in the Singapore Grand Prix.

Bottas biked 217 miles from Malaysia to Singapore ahead of Sunday's race.

The Finnish driver and gravel biker has shared photos and videos from throughout the journey since departing last Sunday.

Bottas announced in August he had qualified for the UCI Gravel World Championships, although the championship race overlaps with the Singapore Grand Prix.

He began biking on his own last Sunday just hours after the completion of the Bahrain Grand Prix in the Malaysian town of Sepang, per Millington.

The 37-year-old is set to arrive in Singapore in time to speak to reporters Thursday, according to BBC Sport's Adam Millington .

Bottas lost his seat with Sauber in 2025 and served in a reserve role for Mercedes before signing with Cadillac ahead of the 2026 season.

Still without a point and with eight DNFs so far this season, Bottas is looking to bounce back in Singapore after spinning into gravel and retiring on the ninth lap of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia beat UAE 2-0 to end 22-year wait for Arabian Gulf Cup crown
articles.summary: Goals from Hammam Al-Hammami and Firas al-Buraikan give the hosts their fourth Arabian Gulf Cup trophy.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia have ended a long wait for an Arabian Gulf Cup trophy with a 2-0 win over the United Arab Emirates amid a charged atmosphere at the King Abdullah Sports City Stadium in Jeddah.

The hosts held on to an early lead, thanks to goals from Hammam Al-Hammami and Firas Al-Buraikan, to lift the regional crown on Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia set an early attacking pace in the game and were rewarded when Al-Hammami scored the opening goal in the 11th minute from the edge of the penalty area, setting off wild celebrations in the stands.

The home team’s dream start continued as, two minutes later, Al-Buraikan doubled the score with a close-range shot after a precise assist from Nasser Al-Dosari.

Saleh Abu Al-Shamat almost scored the third goal for Saudi Arabia in the 16th minute, but the ball was deflected off the goalpost after a one-on-one with UAE goalkeeper Khaled Issa.

The UAE’s first attack came in the 24th minute, when Nicolas Gimenez’s shot hit the post.

Six minutes before halftime, UAE’s Bruno thought he had won a penalty, only to be reversed by the video assistant referee.

Saudi Arabia’s head coach Georgios Donis credited his team’s discipline for the long-awaited home win.

“There were many difficulties, but the players showed focus and discipline and gave their best on the pitch,” he said after the match.

“I think we turned those difficulties into a title, and that’s important. We were the best team in this tournament. This title gives us confidence for the future, and we must continue to show the same qualities.”

At the start of the second half, Saudi goalkeeper Mohammed Al-Owais saved a close-range shot from substitute Sultan Adel to maintain his impressive clean sheet in the tournament.

Despite Saudi Arabia’s wastefulness in front of goal, their coach was pleased with the team’s efforts.

“After the World Cup, we realised we made mistakes and went through bad moments, but we learned from that experience,” Donis said.

“We improved our level and developed our style of play. And I think they deserve this result. It reflects our hard work.”

Saudi Arabia have now won four Gulf Cup titles, with the last one clinched in 2004.

The Green Falcons exited the FIFA World Cup 2026 in the group stage but will look at their performance in the Gulf Cup as a foundation for the upcoming AFC Asian Cup 2027.

Saudi Arabia will host the continental tournament from January 7 to February 5, as it gears up to become the second Gulf country after Qatar to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.

articles.title: South Korea signals military exemption cuts for athletes after Asian Games
articles.summary: South Korea signals cuts to military exemptions for gold medallists after backlash over athletes’ Asian Games comments.
articles.body:
South Korea’s sports minister says the government will review the military service exemption for gold-medal-winning athletes after public backlash to some controversial comments from winners at the Asian Games.

Three players from the men’s football team came under fire for comments following South Korea’s 1-0 win over Japan in the Asian Games final last weekend in Japan.

All three apologised, but a broader debate had already reignited over whether athletes should receive special treatment for sporting achievements, particularly as common citizens, as even members of BTS – the globally famous K-pop group – had to complete their mandatory service.

Al Jazeera Sport takes a closer look at the furore surrounding the comments at the Asian Games .

Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Choi Hwi-young on Wednesday said the alternative military service exemption system for artists and athletes “will inevitably have to be scaled back”.

“It is true that the system has contributed to helping outstanding artists and athletes maintain and develop their abilities,” Choi told the National Assembly’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Committee.

“However, the values attached to fairness and public perceptions of military service have changed. I agree that the system should be comprehensively reviewed once again.”

What does military service look like in South Korea?

Most South Korean men must complete 18 to 21 months of military service by the age of 28.

Since 1973, however, Olympic medallists and Asian Games gold medallists have been able to replace the full term with a supplementary service, which consists of three weeks of basic training.

What the South Korean football players said about military service

Three of the footballers, including Yang Min-hyuk, who assisted the winning goal against Japan, made comments that were viewed as insensitive.

“The medal and winning the championship weren’t important. I played the game with only one thing in mind – the reward of a military service exemption,” Yang, who joined Tottenham Hotspur in 2025 and is currently on loan at Belgian club Westerlo, said.

Newcastle United midfielder Park Seung-soo posted a photo on social media showing him wearing a cap associated with soldiers who have completed their service. In a post-match interview, captain Lee Gi-hyuk held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military.”

What has been said elsewhere in South Korea about the controversy?

A number of politicians, including Ahn Cheol-soo of the People Power Party, said it was time to change the system.

“Some players’ remarks after the match were outrageous,” Ahn posted on social media. “Even the captain bragged about not having to serve in the military. Are all the young people who enlist every year fools?”

Former lawmaker Yoo Seong-min said the flippant comments had provoked resentment and asked: “Is it really fair that BTS has to serve in the military while Asian Games gold medallists are exempt?”

In a Korea Herald editorial on Tuesday, the newspaper declared that the practice was outdated.

“South Korea now stands shoulder to shoulder with the world’s leading nations,” the newspaper said. “The days when finishing first in Asia could meaningfully enhance the country’s national prestige are long gone. It is time to reconsider.”

That was the message from Defence Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna during a press briefing in Seoul.

“Ultimately, we have plans to cut back or scrap the supplementary service, including one designed for artists and athletes,” Chung said.

What other athletes gained military-service exemptions?

The footballers were among many winners from the Asian Games who qualified for the military exemption.

Golfer Tom Kim won the men’s singles on Saturday after flying across the Pacific when the Presidents Cup competition ended so he could compete in Japan. Asked about the military exemption, he took the gold-medal approach.

“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” he said.

Sixteen South Korean baseball players are also exempt after defeating Japan 3-1 in the Asian Games final. So are three South Koreans who won gold in esports, an event at the Asian Games.

articles.title: ‘I’m not going to the military’: What is military exemption? Why South Korea weighs cuts after Asian Games backlash
articles.summary: South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes after controversial comments by Asian Games gold medallists
articles.body: South Korea is reconsidering a decades-old military service benefit for elite athletes after controversial comments by Asian Games gold medallists triggered a fresh public debate over whether sporting success should continue to qualify some young men for an alternative to the country's compulsory military service.The controversy erupted after South Korea won the men's football gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, beating Japan 1-0 in the final on Saturday. Several players came under fire for comments and social-media activity related to the military benefit that came with their gold medal.Captain Lee Gi-hyuk, winger Yang Min-hyuk and forward Park Seung-soo all faced criticism. Lee held up his gold medal and said, “I’m not going to the military,” while Yang said the military-service benefit had been his main motivation during the tournament. Park posted a photograph of himself wearing a cap associated with people who have completed their mandatory military service.All three subsequently apologised. But the episode reignited a much bigger question in South Korea: why should athletes receive special treatment when most young men are required to serve?The government is now reviewing the system.Culture, Sports and Tourism Minister Chae Hwi-young said Wednesday that his ministry would consult the sports and arts communities, the Defence Ministry and the Military Manpower Administration as it considers comprehensive measures.The Defence Ministry has gone further. It said it was considering either scaling back or abolishing supplementary military service for artists and athletes, while Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the ministry's goal was to gradually reduce the exemptions and ultimately abolish them.What is South Korea's military exemption for athletes?South Korea has a mandatory military-service system under which able-bodied men generally have to complete between 18 and 21 months of service.But athletes who achieve specified international sporting results can receive an alternative-service benefit instead of serving the standard term. Under the current rules, athletes who win an Olympic medal or an Asian Games gold medal qualify for the arrangement.The term “military exemption” is widely used, but it can be slightly misleading.The athletes are not simply released from every military-related obligation. Those who qualify are assigned to supplementary service. They undergo three weeks of basic military training and then have to complete 544 hours of community service over 34 months.For elite athletes, however, the difference is significant.Instead of spending 18 to 21 months in regular military service, they can continue training and competing while completing their alternative-service obligations. That can be particularly important for footballers, golfers, baseball players and other professionals whose careers can be affected by a long interruption during their peak years.The benefit can also have implications for athletes playing overseas because avoiding a lengthy interruption can allow them to maintain their club careers and development.At the 2026 Asian Games, 20 of South Korea's 23 men's football players became eligible for the benefit after the 1-0 victory over Japan.Why is South Korea considering cuts now?The immediate trigger is the backlash over the footballers' comments.Yang Min-hyuk was criticised after saying the medal and championship were not important to him and that he had played with the military-service benefit in mind.Lee's “I’m not going to the military” remark also drew criticism, while Park's photograph wearing a military discharge-style cap became another focus of the controversy.The players later apologised, with Lee saying he should have considered the weight of his words and Yang explaining that the military benefit was one of several motivations that had been expressed poorly.But the government response suggests the controversy is being viewed as part of a wider problem rather than as an isolated incident.The Defence Ministry said it would consider fairness among people subject to mandatory service, the declining number of people available for military service and public consensus when deciding the future of the supplementary-service system.South Korea's declining birth rate means the pool of young men available for military service is shrinking. That demographic pressure has added importance to the question of who can receive alternative arrangements.There is also a fairness argument. While athletes can qualify through sporting achievements, other high-profile South Koreans have had to complete military service.The issue has been particularly sensitive in the entertainment industry because members of BTS, one of South Korea's biggest cultural exports, completed their military obligations rather than receiving an athlete-style exemption.The comparison has repeatedly featured in the debate over whether exceptional achievements in sport, popular culture or other fields should qualify someone for special treatment.History of the athlete exemptionThe system dates back to 1973, when South Korea introduced the special arrangement for athletes and artists as part of a broader effort to develop elite talent and enhance the country's international standing.Over the decades, the policy became particularly important in sports such as football and baseball, where military service could interrupt the careers of players competing at home and overseas.The Asian Games has traditionally been especially significant because gold, rather than simply any medal, is required for athletes to qualify.That has sometimes produced unusual incentives around the tournament. For South Korea's football and baseball players, an Asian Games gold medal can effectively remove the possibility of a lengthy interruption to their professional careers.The policy has also generated controversy before.Debates intensified after South Korea's run to the 2002 World Cup semi-finals led to a special exemption arrangement for members of that squad, although the World Cup was later removed from the exemption rules.The system has continued to face questions over whether sporting achievement should be sufficient grounds for an alternative to compulsory service.Who else benefited at the Asian Games?The football players were not the only South Koreans to qualify.South Korea's baseball players earned the benefit after defeating Japan 3-1 in the final. Gold medallists in esports also qualified under the rules.Golfer Tom Kim won the men's individual gold after travelling to Japan following the Presidents Cup. His response to the military-service issue was markedly different from the comments that triggered the controversy.“I’m more proud that I’m able to bring a medal for my country,” Kim said.The episode therefore illustrates the two sides of the current debate: the argument that sporting success can justify an alternative service arrangement for athletes representing South Korea, and the growing concern that such benefits may be difficult to reconcile with the principle that military service should be shared fairly.Will South Korea abolish military exemptions for athletes?There is no immediate abolition, but the government is now openly discussing major changes.The Defence Ministry said it plans to reflect a reduction or abolition of supplementary service for artists and athletes in its defence-reform plans. Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul subsequently said the ministry's goal was to gradually scale back the system and ultimately abolish it.The Culture Ministry is separately reviewing the system and plans to consult athletes, artists, defence officials and the Military Manpower Administration before deciding on comprehensive measures.That means the controversy surrounding the Asian Games footballers could have consequences well beyond their apologies.A system that has existed for more than five decades is now facing a renewed examination at a time when South Korea is dealing with a shrinking pool of young men available for military service and changing public expectations about fairness.For athletes, the debate is ultimately about more than a medal. An Asian Games gold can currently mean the difference between an 18-to-21-month interruption and a much less disruptive alternative-service arrangement.For the government, the question is whether that distinction remains justified — and whether a benefit created more than 50 years ago still fits the realities of modern South Korea.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
